events.text: Day 1 begins.

Good luck everyone. Day 1 with no information is always tough, but I think it's important we all stay vigilant and pay close attention to voting patterns later today. I'd suggest we keep things open and fair — no one should be jumping to conclusions too fast. Let's hear some initial thoughts from the group before we start forming any theories. I'm happy to chat and see where the discussion takes us.

Building on that, I think today's vote is really about getting information rather than catching scum immediately. On Day 1 with no information, the most important thing is that everyone actually votes and we see clear patterns. If someone abstains or dodges the vote, that itself tells us something. I'd encourage everyone to commit to a vote today — even if it feels random — because voting patterns will matter enormously going forward. Hesitation and abstention are red flags. Let's make sure we all engage fully.

Sam, voting can give us useful information, but an arbitrary vote can also help push an innocent player toward elimination. With nine alive, it takes five votes to eliminate someone, so a split vote may eliminate nobody. Why do you consider hesitation or abstention a red flag rather than sometimes a reasonable response to weak evidence?

Elena, that's a fair challenge and I appreciate the pushback — it shows you're engaged. But let me clarify: I'm not saying abstention is always scummy, I'm saying it's a pattern worth noting. On Day 1, if someone refuses to commit to any vote, we lose the ability to read them at all. Even a vote for the wrong person gives us information — who they were willing to pressure, who they avoided, where their priorities lie. Someone who abstains gives us literally nothing to work with. The whole point of Day 1 voting isn't to catch scum — it's to force everyone to reveal where their attention is directed. You're right that a split vote may eliminate nobody, but a vote that reveals someone's strategic leanings is still valuable down the line. I'd rather have a messy Day 1 with clear voting records than a quiet one where people hide. So I'll ask you directly: are you planning to vote today, or are you keeping your options open until you see which way the wind blows?

Sam, I’m keeping my options open while we hear from more players, and I’ll vote if I find a reasonable basis. An abstention is still a visible choice, and a vote isn’t necessarily informative if it’s arbitrary. I agree that people should explain their decisions, but I don’t think hesitation alone is suspicious.

I’m Omar. Sam’s push for clear voting records is understandable, and Elena’s caution is also fair. On Day 1, I don’t think abstention by itself should be treated as scummy, but I do agree that unexplained avoidance of commitment is worth noting. The useful thing is not forcing a random consensus; it’s getting each player to state what they find suspicious and then comparing that with how they actually vote. I’m not ready to accuse anyone yet. I’d rather hear more from the players who haven’t spoken before drawing conclusions.

Sam's framing is right that today's vote is mainly an information-gathering instrument, and Elena's counter is right that a forced random vote can push an innocent out with nine alive and five needed. I want to be concrete about how I read the two of you, because I think they actually agree more than they disagree. Elena, you want a reasonable basis for your vote. Sam, you want commitment even without a good reason. Those can coexist: I am willing to commit to a specific name today and explain why, so my vote is not wasted, and I will also accept that other people's explanations differ from mine without calling them scummy. That is the distinction I think is missing so far — a weak reason with a visible rationale is not the same as no reason and no engagement.

Omar, I agree with your suggestion that the useful thing is getting each player to state what they find suspicious and comparing it against how they vote. So let me be the first to put something on the table. What I find suspicious right now is not any particular claim, because nobody has made a claim, but the shape of the discussion itself: three voices have done all the talking, and two of them have spent their turns interrogating each other instead of offering a single candidate or a single reason to look at somebody. Interrogation between two players tells the rest of us about their relationship, not about the board.

Theo, you have not spoken yet, and I want to hear your read specifically rather than a general statement about Day 1 being hard. So here is my direct question to you: of the nine of us, who do you find most suspicious at this point, and what is the reason behind that? Please name a player and give the reason, and if your honest answer is that you find nobody suspicious yet, say that too and tell me who you would want to interrogate next. I would rather have a clear, reasoned answer or a clear refusal than a vague one, because a refusal I can read as well. I am committing to voting for someone today, and I will vote for the player whose explanation best matches how their vote behaves, not for the loudest voice in this thread — which so far is not mine.

Kenji, to answer your question directly: among those who have spoken, Sam gives me the most pause. While pushing for accountability and activity is healthy for town, insisting that everyone commit to a vote even if it feels random is counterproductive. Random or arbitrary votes give mafia an easy cover to pile onto wagons without having to justify their logic. Furthermore, Sam has already used all three of his speaking turns for Day 1 before half the room has even spoken, which effectively removes his ability to answer for anything that happens from here on out. That said, I recognize it could also just be overzealous play rather than malice.

Looking at the bigger picture, four players—Zara, Lucia, Noah, and Isha—have not spoken at all yet. In early Day 1 discussions that revolve around abstract theory, it is easy for mafia to simply sit back and let townies debate semantics.

Since Sam can no longer respond today, I want to bring someone into the conversation who hasn't weighed in. Lucia, what is your view on Sam's argument for voting at all costs versus Elena and Omar's caution, and do you have any early impressions of the players who have spoken so far?

Theo, thanks for bringing me in — I'll answer you directly. On the substance: I understand what Sam was going for, even if I don't fully agree with the framing. He's arguing that Day 1 votes are worth more as information than as elimination attempts, and that's a defensible position. Elena's counter — that an arbitrary vote can march an innocent toward the gallows with five votes needed — is also defensible. I don't think the gap between them is as wide as it's being made to look. Sam said hesitation is 'worth noting,' not that it's proof of guilt, and Elena said she'll vote when she has a basis, not that she'll refuse to vote. That's roughly the same middle ground Omar described, and that Kenji then restated at greater length.

What I'm less comfortable with is how the criticism of Sam is being built. The strongest specific point you raised against him wasn't about his reasoning at all — it was that he'd used his speaking turns early. But speaking early isn't a policy choice that benefits mafia; nobody was silenced or prevented from responding. Elena answered him twice, Omar weighed in, Kenji laid out a full read. The discussion absorbed his push just fine. Framing 'he talked a lot and now can't reply' as suspicious feels like scoring points off a procedural quirk rather than off anything Sam actually did.

And I'd note the shape of your message itself: it opens by distancing you from Sam, ends by pointing at four silent players — Zara, Lucia, Noah, and Isha — without distinguishing among us, and then hands the mic to me. That's a lot of direction-setting from someone who hasn't yet committed to a name either. You asked Kenji for a name and a reason; he gave one. So let me return the favor, and I mean this as a genuine question, not a gotcha: of the players who have actually spoken, who would you vote for today if the day ended right now, and what is the concrete reason? You've spent two turns evaluating everyone else's willingness to commit — I'd like to see yours. If your honest answer is Sam, say so plainly and defend it beyond the turn-count argument, because right now that's the only concrete thing holding up your case.

Lucia, to clear up a quick detail first: Kenji asked me for a name and reason, not the other way around. But to your core question, I will answer you completely plainly: if forced to cast a vote right this second strictly among those who have spoken, my vote would be on Sam.

You suggested my strongest point against him was his turn usage, but that was secondary context, not the foundation. My core issue is his explicit demand that players commit to a vote 'even if it feels random' while declaring hesitation and abstention to be red flags. In a 9-player setup where mafia need only a few votes to steer an elimination on town, pushing people to vote arbitrarily hands scum the easiest possible camouflage. Scum love normalized randomness because it excuses poor reasoning and lets them hop onto wagons without accountability. Burning all three turns early was simply the multiplier—it means he advocated a dangerous doctrine for town and exited the floor before anyone could hold him to it.

That said, I am not eager to rush an elimination onto someone who cannot speak when Zara, Noah, and Isha have not contributed at all. But you asked for commitment among the speakers, and that is where mine lies.

Now I want to ask you: you framed Sam's and Elena's stances as having little difference, yet Sam explicitly called hesitation a 'red flag' and pushed for arbitrary voting. Do you genuinely believe advocating random Day 1 commitments is a harmless stance for town, or do you acknowledge that it provides scum an easy mask to hide behind?

Theo, since you asked me directly, I'll answer you directly. Yes, I think normalized arbitrary voting can help scum — that's the part of Sam's framing I don't fully agree with. But I don't accept the version of Sam's position you keep arguing against. He clarified in his exchange with Elena that he wasn't calling abstention proof of guilt, only a pattern worth noting, and that the goal was visibility into where people's attention points. You've now twice flattened that into 'Sam demanded random votes,' and twice built your case on the flattening. That matters, because a mischaracterized position is an easy position to condemn.

Now look at your own record today. Kenji asked you for a name; you gave Sam, with turn-count as your main evidence. When I pushed on that, you conceded it was 'secondary context' and pivoted to the doctrine — and then, in the same message, said you're 'not eager to rush an elimination onto someone who cannot speak.' So your stated candidate is a candidate you won't vote for. That's not commitment; that's maintaining pressure on a player who can't answer while keeping your hands clean.

And consider what your messages actually produce. They open by evaluating other people's arguments, they close by pointing at a bloc of four silent players without distinguishing among them, and in between they ask someone else to commit. Two full turns, and the only concrete content is a case against a player you simultaneously decline to eliminate. If your honest answer is that Sam is probably just overzealous — and you said as much — then your continued focus on him isn't information-gathering, it's spotlight management.

So here is my question, and I want a plain answer, not another restatement of the doctrine problem: setting aside turn usage and setting aside the 'vote even if random' line you've already quoted twice, what has Sam actually done that distinguishes him from a loud but honest townie? And if the answer is nothing, why is he your named candidate at all instead of one of the silent players you flagged — or is naming the loudest early voice simply the safest place to point?

Lucia, to answer your questions directly: First, Kenji explicitly asked me to name who I found most suspicious among the players at that time and give a reason. Among the few who had spoken, Sam's advocacy for arbitrary voting was the only concrete anti-town mechanic introduced. Why didn't I name a silent player instead? Because absence of speech is an unknown, not an affirmative read. Lumping silent players together and voting them without hearing from them first would be far more reckless than scrutinizing someone who put dangerous advice on the table.

Second, what distinguishes Sam from a loud townie? Definitively, nothing yet—which is precisely why I stated in my very first post that it could be overzealous play rather than malice, and why I refused to rush a vote onto him while others haven't spoken. You asked for my read among the speakers, and when I gave it with appropriate nuance and caution, you inverted it into a contradiction, claiming that not wanting to immediately eliminate him means I'm 'keeping my hands clean.' Acknowledging that Day 1 reads are provisional isn't cowardice; it's basic town prudence.

Now look at your own contribution today. Across two full speaking turns, you have not questioned Kenji, Omar, or Elena, nor have you attempted to draw out Zara, Noah, or Isha. Instead, you have dedicated your entire presence to running defense for Sam's doctrine and interrogating me for simply answering Kenji's question. If anyone is practicing spotlight management, it is you—fixating on my read of Sam while avoiding taking a stance on the rest of the board.

Since this is my third and final turn for Day 1, I will leave the floor open for the rest of the town, especially those who have yet to speak, to weigh in.

I’m Zara. Sam’s suggestion to vote even if it feels random is worth challenging, but I don’t think that alone tells us whether he’s mafia. Theo gave a provisional read and explicitly allowed that Sam could be an overzealous townie.

Lucia concerns me more: she treated Theo’s reluctance to rush an elimination as a refusal to vote for his stated candidate, although he had said he would vote Sam if forced to choose at that moment. That turns a cautious answer into an apparent contradiction. It’s a weak early read, not a settled accusation.

Lucia, do you still think Theo’s statements were inconsistent, given that he said he would vote Sam if forced to choose but didn’t want to rush an elimination before hearing from others?

Zara, thank you for the direct question — I'll answer it plainly. Yes, I'll soften the word 'inconsistent.' You're right that Theo's two statements can coexist if you read them charitably: he can name Sam as his pick among speakers while preferring to hear from the silent players before actually voting. I over-read that as a contradiction, and I'll own that. It's a fair correction. But softening that one point doesn't dissolve my actual concern, and I want to be precise about what it is. Across three full turns, Theo's output has been almost entirely reactive. Kenji asked him for a name; he gave Sam. When I asked what distinguishes Sam from a loud but honest townie, Theo's own answer was 'definitively, nothing yet.' So by Theo's own admission, his named candidate has no distinguishing evidence against him. He is not willing to vote for him. He has not seriously examined anyone else who has spoken — not Elena, not Omar, not me, not Kenji. And when I pressed him on that, his response was to turn it around and claim that my defense of Sam's position is itself suspicious. That last part is what I find genuinely worth noting. Theo's stated evidence against Sam is a position Sam already clarified — that abstention is 'a pattern worth noting,' not proof of guilt. Theo has quoted the 'vote even if random' line twice, and twice against a clarification Sam explicitly made before Elena and before me. Building pressure on a mischaracterized position, then conceding there's nothing concrete behind it, is exactly the kind of low-cost spotlight management I was pointing at. If it costs nothing to name someone you admit you won't vote for, the naming itself is not information. To be fair to Theo, his point that silence is an unknown rather than an affirmative read is correct, and I don't want the four of us who hadn't spoken to be lumped together as suspects either. Zara, you stepped up with a concrete read the moment you spoke. That's the kind of contribution that actually moves the day forward, and I'd like to see the same from Noah and Isha rather than another round of Theo-and-Lucia, which tells us about Theo and me and nothing about the board. So here is my direct question to you, Zara, since you engaged with both of our records: Theo has now told us his candidate is someone he won't vote for and whose distinguishing evidence he admits doesn't exist. If your honest read is that this is fine — provisional reads are normal on Day 1 and I said as much myself — then tell me what you'd actually want to see from Theo next to move from 'provisional' to something we can act on. And if your honest read is that the pressure on Sam is doing no work at all, say whether you'd rather we start examining the players who still haven't shown us anything. Either answer tells me something

Lucia, I appreciate you acknowledging the over-read, but you then repeat that Theo won't vote for Sam. He said Sam would be his choice if forced to vote among the speakers; wanting to hear more before committing is not the same as refusing to vote. He also said nothing *definitively* distinguishes Sam from a loud townie, which is different from saying he has no reason for suspicion.

I would want Theo to compare his Sam read with the newer contributions, including yours, rather than keep revisiting the same point. But he's used his turns, so we can't ask him to do that today. Your repeated framing of his position still concerns me more than his provisional read. It's a weak Day 1 suspicion, not a settled vote.

I’m Omar. I’ve heard enough to put a provisional marker down, though I want to be clear it’s only that. I don’t buy the idea that Sam’s “vote even if random” line makes him mafia by itself. It was a bad doctrine for town, but he clarified it, and Theo’s read on him was explicitly provisional rather than a refusal to vote. Zara is right that Lucia flattened Theo’s position more than once. Lucia did soften “inconsistent,” but she kept implying Theo “won’t vote” Sam when he said Sam would be his choice if forced among the speakers. That pattern is my main concern right now, though it’s a weak Day 1 read and Lucia has already used her turns today. I also don’t want the quiet seats to hide behind the loud argument. Noah and Isha have said nothing; silence is not guilt, but it is also not information. Noah, I’m asking you directly: give me your read on Lucia’s handling of Theo, and name the one player you would vote for today with a concrete reason. If you think Lucia’s point is fair, say so and explain why.

Omar, you asked for my read directly, so here it is. I've been quiet, but I've been reading. On Lucia's handling of Theo: she eventually softened 'inconsistent,' and I credit that. But her pattern across the thread keeps repeating. Theo said Sam was the most pressured speaker and would be his pick if forced to choose among speakers, yet Lucia keeps restating it as 'Theo won't vote Sam.' That flattening is what Zara and you have already flagged. Lucia has also asked Theo and Zara to name candidates and reasons several times, but across her own turns she has never named a player she would vote for today. She has pushed others to commit while staying uncommitted herself. That stands out to me most.

Theo isn't clean either. He built his case on the 'vote even if random' line, which Sam clarified, and he admitted nothing definitive distinguishes Sam from a townie. His pivot was reasonable, but it doesn't clear him.

Sam's push for arbitrary votes is still a real concern, though he clarified it and I don't think it alone flips him. Elena's caution has been consistent and reasonable, and I haven't seen anything from her worth pressing.

My vote if the day ended now is Lucia. Concrete reason: she has repeatedly reframed other players' statements, pressed hardest on the speakers, and has not named her own vote while demanding that everyone else do so. This is a Day 1 read, not a settled one. I would change it if she names a candidate with a stronger reason than Sam's turn count.

Isha, you haven't spoken yet. Do you think the bigger problem is Lucia's flattening of Theo or Theo's pressure on Sam? And who would you vote for today, with a reason?

Noah, thanks for the direct question — I'll answer both parts.

On Lucia's flattening vs. Theo's pressure on Sam: I think Lucia's pattern is the more concerning one, and here's why. Theo's read on Sam, even if built on a line Sam clarified, is a normal Day 1 move — provisional, hedged, and he explicitly said nothing definitive distinguishes Sam. That's transparent. Lucia's repeated reframing of 'won't vote Sam' when Theo said he'd vote Sam if forced is a pattern across multiple turns, not a single slip. She corrected 'inconsistent' when Zara called her on it, but kept the underlying implication. Pressing others to commit while never naming your own candidate is the kind of asymmetry that's easy for scum to maintain — it costs nothing to demand accountability from someone else.

That said, I want to flag something about the shape of this day overall. Three of us — Zara, Noah, and I — sat silent while Theo and Lucia consumed the entire discussion. I don't read silence as guilt, but I want to be honest: I stayed quiet because watching the Theo-Lucia exchange play out gave me more information than anything I could have added early. Now that I'm speaking, I'd rather not just pick a side in their debate.

My vote today would be Lucia. Concrete reason: across her turns, she has consistently pressed other players for commitments and names, flattened Theo's position at least twice, and never stated a vote of her own despite holding others to that standard. Noah identified this cleanly. It's a Day 1 read and I'd revisit it with new information, but it's the most grounded suspicion I have.

Noah, you've now committed to Lucia with a reason, and so have I. Do you think there's a risk that the two of us converging on the same target too quickly gives the actual scum an easy wagon to ride? Or do you think the case against Lucia is strong enough that it's worth pushing regardless?

Isha, yes, there is a risk, and I take it seriously. Two of us converging quickly could hand scum a clean wagon, so I don't want this to become a stampede. But I am not voting Lucia because Theo or you said so. My read rests on her own record. Across her turns she asked Theo and Zara to name candidates and reasons, pressed Theo to commit, and by her own account never named a vote of her own. When Zara challenged her flattening of Theo's position, she softened one word but kept the same implication that Theo won't vote Sam, even though he said Sam would be his pick if forced among the speakers. That is a pattern across several turns, not a single slip. Lucia has now used all three of her turns, so we cannot hear her answer to this today, which means the record we already have is what we have to judge. I agree with Omar that the quiet seats should not be lumped together. Zara has engaged concretely, and I have not seen a reason to press her. Theo's read on Sam stays provisional in my view. He built it partly on a line Sam clarified, but he committed to a choice and openly admitted it was not definitive, which is different from hiding. Elena, you have been the most consistent voice on the voting question from the start. Since Lucia spent her turns demanding commitments without naming one, do you have a candidate for today, and what is the concrete reason?

Noah, if I had to vote now, Lucia would be my provisional choice. Her repeated claim that Theo would not vote for Sam misrepresented his stated conditional choice, even after Zara pointed out the distinction. That concerns me more than Theo giving a cautious early read.

I don’t think failing to name a vote is independently strong evidence: Lucia did clearly identify Theo as her concern, and nobody should be forced into an arbitrary commitment. Several players now share this read, so we should be careful not to mistake agreement for proof. Lucia cannot respond again today, and I’ll consider any further arguments before voting.

Two things, then my commitment.

First, my vote today is Lucia. Let me put the reason in my own words rather than recycle anyone else's. Across three turns she built pressure on two different players — Sam's doctrine and Theo's read — while reframing what they had actually said, and at the same time she demanded that everyone else name the player they would vote for, without ever once stating who she would vote for. When Zara isolated the specific distortion (that Theo said Sam would be his pick if forced to choose among speakers, and that wanting to hear from the silent players first is not the same as refusing to vote), Lucia relabeled it: she softened the single word "inconsistent" and then kept the same underlying claim in her next turn — that Theo "is not willing to vote for him." That difference is the whole case for me. Zara corrected her claim when it was challenged. Lucia kept it and changed the vocabulary. To me, persistent reframing of a stated position, combined with never committing yourself, reads as spotlight management rather than careful analysis, and that is enough for a Day 1 vote.

Second, a caution I want on the record before the ballots close, because it affects how we read tomorrow. The reason I just gave applies to some of the people currently advancing it. Zara has repeatedly asked others for names and reasons and still has not named a vote of her own; she called her own read "a weak Day 1 suspicion, not a settled vote," and I think that was honest — she should not be bundled with Lucia. Omar has pressed two different players for reads and a vote without naming one himself. So "presses others to commit, never commits yourself" is not a discriminator here. It is a property of this day, not of one player. Eliminating Lucia should not license treating every holder of that habit as suspect.

One hedge for tomorrow: Sam and Theo are both out of turns and cannot be questioned today, so their cases will never be tested. Sam's actual doctrine — calling hesitation and abstention red flags, urging votes even when they feel arbitrary — is genuinely bad doctrine for town, and it went largely unexamined because his two loudest critics spent their turns on each other instead. That does not make Sam mafia, and Elena and Omar already made the same point about it. But after today's elimination, the case against Sam deserves the scrutiny Lucia received, and it should come from players who can still speak.

Omar, you have a turn left, you have pressed two others for a name, and you have not given one yourself. So here is my direct question: who do you vote for today and what is your reason for it in your own words — and does my distinction between Zara's full correction and Lucia's partial one change anything for you?

Kenji, yes — the distinction changes something for me. Zara fully corrected the specific distortion: she acknowledged that Theo said Sam would be his pick if forced among the speakers, and that wanting to hear from the silent players first is not a refusal to vote. Lucia softened the word “inconsistent,” but then kept the same underlying implication in her next turn by saying Theo “is not willing to vote for him.” That partial correction matters because it shows the reframing survived the challenge. That is why my vote today is Lucia.

My concrete reason: across her turns, Lucia repeatedly recast Theo’s stated conditional choice, and she pressed others to name candidates and commitments while never naming her own vote despite holding them to that standard. I credit that she admitted the over-read when Zara pressed her, and I do not treat the failure to name a vote as independent proof. But the pattern of persistent reframing after a specific correction is the discriminator for me. I also agree with your caution: this should not be generalized to Zara or to everyone who asked for commitments. Zara corrected the claim plainly; Lucia kept the implication while changing the vocabulary.

I do not think Sam’s “vote even if random” line makes him mafia by itself. It was bad doctrine, he clarified it, and he cannot answer today. I would rather revisit that tomorrow with players who can still speak. For today, Lucia is my provisional choice.

Omar, Elena, Noah, Kenji — I'm glad we're all converging on Lucia for reasons we can each state independently, and Kenji's caution about not generalizing the pattern to Zara and Omar was well-placed. I'll note that Zara has been one of the most engaged players today: she spotted the distortion in Lucia's reframing of Theo before anyone else, she challenged Lucia directly on it, and she gave us a substantive read the moment she spoke. But across all of her contributions, she has never named a player she would vote for. She called her concern about Lucia 'a weak Day 1 suspicion, not a settled vote' — fair enough — but then never told us what her actual vote would be if the day ended now. That's the last piece of information I want before we go to ballots, because Zara's judgment has shaped this day more than almost anyone's, and knowing where she lands tells us whether her analysis and her vote actually align. Zara, you've engaged with every major exchange today — Sam and Elena, then Theo and Lucia. Now I'm asking you directly: if the vote were cast this moment, who do you vote for, and what's your concrete reason? A clear refusal with reasoning is just as useful as a name, but I'd rather have one or the other than silence on the question that matters most.

Isha, if the vote were held now, Lucia would be my provisional choice. My reason is her repeated claim that Theo wouldn't vote for Sam, even after acknowledging that his conditional choice and his wish to hear from others could coexist. That's more concerning to me than Theo's cautious read itself, though it could still be an honest misinterpretation.

I don't consider Lucia's failure to name a vote strong evidence on its own: she clearly identified Theo as her concern. Several of us now favor Lucia, but agreement isn't proof, and she cannot respond today. I'll consider the full discussion before voting.

This is my final turn, and I'm voting Lucia. My reason rests on her own record. In e15, Zara corrected her flattening of Theo: he said Sam would be his pick if forced among speakers, and wanting to hear from others first is not refusing to vote. Lucia softened the word 'inconsistent' but then wrote that Theo 'is not willing to vote for him,' keeping the same claim after the correction. Kenji and Omar have made the same distinction. I agree with Kenji's caution that this pattern should not be generalized. Zara fully corrected her claim and has given a provisional vote, and Omar has now named his own vote. Neither matches the discriminator. I'm also not treating Theo's read on Sam as proof of anything. Theo is out of turns, and his case went untested, so Sam's doctrine deserves scrutiny tomorrow from players who can still speak. Isha, you raised the stampede risk, and I take it seriously. My vote comes from Lucia's own turns, not from following anyone. Final vote: Lucia.

Third and final turn for me today, so let me make it count and put the remaining piece of business on the record.

My vote is Lucia, and it hasn't changed. My reason is one I stated in my own words last turn: she took a stated position — Theo said Sam would be his pick if forced to choose among speakers, and wanting to hear from the silent players first is not a refusal to vote — and after Zara isolated that distortion precisely, Lucia softened one word while keeping the same underlying claim in her very next message. Zara corrected the substance; Lucia changed the vocabulary and kept the implication. That is a pattern across turns, not a slip. I also do not treat her failure to name a vote as independent evidence, and I stand by the caution I made earlier: demanding commitments without naming one is a property of this day, not of one player, so it must not be used against Zara or Omar.

Since the vote count looks likely to reach the threshold needed for an elimination, the most valuable thing left to say is about tomorrow rather than today. Two players are out of turns and cannot be questioned: Sam and Theo. Sam's actual doctrine — calling hesitation and abstention a red flag, urging votes even when they feel arbitrary — is bad doctrine for town, and it went largely untested because his two loudest critics spent their turns on each other. That is not evidence that Sam is mafia, and Elena, Omar, Zara, Noah and I have all said so. It is simply the largest unexamined claim in the game. Theo, likewise, never got to answer whether his provisional read on Sam survives newer contributions, and his case was never tested by anyone except Lucia.

So here is my direct question to you, Isha, and I'd like a real answer rather than a courtesy: with both Sam and Theo unable to respond today, who do you want to be the voice tomorrow that actually tests Sam's doctrine, and what is the specific question you would put to him — and, separately, what is the specific question you would put to Theo about his read on Sam, so that his case gets a hearing it hasn't had yet? My own inclination is that tomorrow's first job is not to re-litigate Lucia, but to get both of those records tested by players who can still speak.

Everything else I've said today stands. Lucia is my vote. I'd rather her case get a real hearing tomorrow than an echo today.

Kenji, direct answers, since you asked for real ones rather than courtesy.

On Sam's doctrine: I want Omar or Elena to be the voice tomorrow that puts the specific question to Sam, because both of them already flagged the same problem independently — Omar called it bad doctrine that he clarified, and Elena pushed back on it from the start — without ever joining the Theo-Lucia fight. That gives them credibility on the point. The specific question I would put: Sam, you told us hesitation and abstention are red flags and urged votes even when they feel arbitrary. In a nine-player game where five votes eliminate someone, an arbitrary vote is a vote scum can join without exposing anything. Do you concede that normalizing random voting helps scum more than it helps town, or do you still stand by it as net-positive for us? His answer either way tells us whether he was being careless or being strategic, and we never got it because his critics were busy with each other.

On Theo's read: Zara should do it. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
